title: Athamas et Ino
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Bacchus is a god in Thebes now, and Ino — his mother's sister, who nursed him — carries her head high; Juno cannot bear it, and goes down the yew-dark road to the underworld herself to set a Fury on the house. Tisiphone comes up with a blood-soaked torch and a poison that leaves the body unmarked and works only on the mind, and Athamas, seeing a lioness where his wife is, kills his small son; Ino carries the other child over a cliff into the sea. Venus asks her uncle Neptune for the two of them, and they come up as the sea-gods Leucothoe and Palaemon, while the Theban women who mourned them are caught mid-gesture and fixed there. It opens with Juno reciting Bacchus's victories against her in her own voice, and closes on the shore with the mourners held in whatever posture the change found them in — some of them stone, some of them already birds over the water.

sentences.t:
Tum vero totis Bacchi memorabile Thebis
numen erat, magnasque novi matertera vires
narrat ubique dei, de totque sororibus expers
una doloris erat, nisi quem fecere sorores.
sentences.l: Then indeed the divine power of Bacchus was a thing to be spoken of throughout all Thebes, and his mother's sister tells everywhere the great strength of the new god, and out of so many sisters she alone was free of grief — except such grief as her sisters had made.
sentences.i: Then indeed the godhead of Bacchus was on every tongue in Thebes, and his mother's sister told everywhere of the new god's great power; of so many sisters she alone was untouched by grief — except the grief her sisters had made.
sentences.n: `fecere` is `fecerunt`, the poetic third-plural perfect: Ovid uses the short `-ēre` ending for `-ērunt` constantly, for the metre, and it is the same tense either way. `matertera` is exact — the sister on the mother's side — and it is the whole reason Juno is about to be interested in Ino. `expers` takes a genitive, `doloris`, and the last clause takes it straight back.

sentences.t:
Adspicit hanc natis thalamoque Athamantis habentem
sublimes animos et alumno numine Iuno,
nec tulit, et secum
sentences.l: Juno looks upon her, holding lofty spirits because of her children and the marriage-chamber of Athamas and because of the divine power she had nursed, and she did not bear it, and to herself [she said]:
sentences.i: Juno saw her carrying her head high — her children, her marriage to Athamas, the god she had nursed — and could not bear it, and said to herself:
sentences.n: Three ablatives of cause hang on `habentem sublimes animos`: `natis`, `thalamo`, `alumno numine`. `alumnum numen` is 'the godhead she reared' — Bacchus, whom Ino nursed — and it is the item on the list that makes her intolerable. No verb of speaking is written: Latin often leaves `dixit` to be supplied before a quotation, and English has to put it in.

sentences.t:
“potuit de paelice natus
vertere Maeonios pelagoque inmergere nautas
et laceranda suae nati dare viscera matri
et triplices operire novis Minyeidas alis:
sentences.l: 'The one born from the mistress was able to turn the Maeonian sailors and to plunge them in the sea, and to give a son's flesh to that son's own mother to be torn, and to cover the three daughters of Minyas with new wings:
sentences.i: 'A mistress's son could transform the Maeonian sailors and sink them in the sea, could hand a son's flesh to the son's own mother to tear, could cover the three daughters of Minyas with new-made wings:
sentences.n: `paelex` is the other woman — a mistress, a kept woman — and it is Juno's word, not the poem's: she will not name Semele, and she will not name Bacchus either, who gets only 'the one born from'. `vertere` stands with no complement at all — the bare verb of change, with the new shape left unsaid — and the three deeds she lists are all told earlier in the poem, the daughters of Minyas only a few pages back in this same book. `laceranda ... viscera` is a gerundive of purpose after `dare`: flesh handed over *to be torn*.

sentences.t:
nil poterit Iuno nisi inultos flere dolores?
idque mihi satis est? haec una potentia nostra est?
sentences.l: 'Will Juno be able [to do] nothing except weep for griefs unavenged? and is that enough for me? is this our one power?'
sentences.i: 'Will Juno be able to do nothing but weep over griefs unavenged? And is that enough for me? Is this the one power I have?'
sentences.n: Juno speaks of herself in the third person and by name, measuring herself against her own reputation. `nil` is the internal object of `poterit` and the only infinitive left standing is `flere`, rescued by the `nisi` — 'will be able to do nothing except weep' — so the single thing she can still manage is the one the sentence grants her grudgingly. The sting is in the adjective `inultos`: not grief, but grief with nothing done about it.

sentences.t:
ipse docet, quid agam (fas est et ab hoste doceri),
quidque furor valeat, Penthea caede satisque
ac super ostendit:
sentences.l: 'He himself teaches what I am to do (it is right to be taught even by an enemy), and what frenzy is worth he has shown, by the killing of Pentheus, enough and beyond:
sentences.i: 'He himself is teaching me what to do — it is right to be taught even by an enemy — and what frenzy is worth he has shown, in Pentheus's killing, enough and to spare:
sentences.n: `fas est et ab hoste doceri` is one of the lines of this poem that travels on its own, and two words carry it: `et` here is 'even', not 'and', and `fas` is what divine law allows rather than what a statute permits. `quid agam` is a deliberative subjunctive inside an indirect question, 'what I am to do'. `Penthea` is not the Greek accusative of the name here but the adjective `Pentheus, -a, -um` in the ablative agreeing with `caede`, 'by the Penthean killing' — Ovid coins adjectives off proper names freely, and does it twice more in this part at 497. `satis ac super` is a set phrase, 'enough and over'.

sentences.t:
cur non stimuletur eatque
per cognata suis exempla furoribus Ino?”
sentences.l: 'why should Ino not be goaded, and go through the examples of her own kin by means of frenzies of her own?'
sentences.i: 'why should Ino not be spurred on, and travel the road her kin have travelled, driven by frenzies of her own?'
sentences.n: `stimuletur` and `eat` are deliberative subjunctives again, asking what is to be done rather than what is the case. `per cognata exempla` makes her family's madnesses a road she can be made to walk. Juno's target is named in the last word of the speech, which is where Latin likes to put the person it has been circling.

sentences.t:
Est via declivis funesta nubila taxo,
ducit ad infernas per muta silentia sedes.
Styx nebulas exhalat iners, umbraeque recentes
descendunt illac simulacraque functa sepulcris.
sentences.l: There is a way sloping downward, clouded with the deadly yew; it leads to the seats below through mute silences. Sluggish Styx breathes out mists, and the fresh shades go down that way, and the phantoms that have discharged their tombs.
sentences.i: There is a road that runs downhill, dim with the deadly yew, and it leads through mute silence to the dwellings below. Sluggish Styx breathes mist, and by that road the newly dead go down, ghosts that have had their burial.
sentences.n: `Est via` — 'there is a road' — is Ovid's standing formula for opening a set-piece of scenery, and everything that follows is description until Juno steps into it. `funesta nubila taxo` is an ablative of cause with the adjective split from its noun across the line; the yew is the tree of funerals. `functa sepulcris` is the deponent `fungor` with the ablative it governs, 'having performed the rites of the tomb': only the buried may go down.

sentences.t:
Pallor hiemsque tenent late loca senta, novique,
qua sit iter, manes, Stygiam qua ducat ad urbem,
ignorant, ubi sit nigri fera regia Ditis.
sentences.l: Pallor and winter hold the bristling places far and wide, and the new shades do not know where the road is, where it leads to the Stygian city, where the wild palace of black Dis is.
sentences.i: Pallor and winter hold those bristling wastes far and wide, and the newly arrived ghosts do not know where the road runs, or where it leads to the Stygian city, or where black Dis has his savage hall.
sentences.n: Three indirect questions in a row, each with a subjunctive verb (`sit`, `ducat`, `sit`), and all of them governed by an `ignorant` that Ovid holds back to the head of the third line — the bewilderment arrives before the word for it. `novi ... manes` is split around the whole first question. Magnus prints `qua ducat`, 'by what way it leads'; some editions print `quod ducat`, 'which leads'.

sentences.t:
Mille capax aditus et apertas undique portas
urbs habet, utque fretum de tota flumina terra,
sic omnes animas locus accipit ille, nec ulli
exiguus populo est, turbamve accedere sentit.
sentences.l: The roomy city has a thousand approaches and gates open on every side, and as the sea [takes] rivers from the whole earth, so that place takes all souls, and it is not too small for any people, nor does it feel a crowd arriving.
sentences.i: The city is capacious: a thousand ways in, and gates standing open on every side; and as the sea takes the rivers of the whole earth, so that place takes every soul — never cramped by any nation, never feeling a crowd come in.
sentences.n: The simile's first half has no verb: `ut fretum ... flumina` borrows the `accipit` of the second half, an economy Latin allows and English needs a bracket for. `nec ulli exiguus populo est` is a dative of reference, 'not small for any people', and the understatement is the point — hell has room. `capax` is placed next to `Mille`, so the size lands in the first two words.

sentences.t:
Errant exsangues sine corpore et ossibus umbrae,
parsque forum celebrant, pars imi tecta tyranni,
pars aliquas artes, antiquae imitamina vitae.
exercent, aliam partem sua poena coercet
sentences.l: Bloodless shades wander without body and bones, and part throng the forum, part the halls of the lowest tyrant, part ply some craft or other, imitations of their former life; another part its own punishment holds fast.
sentences.i: Bloodless shades drift about, without body, without bone: some crowd the forum, some the halls of the tyrant below, some ply a trade of one kind or another, imitations of the life they had; another part its punishment keeps.
sentences.n: `pars ... celebrant` takes a plural verb by sense rather than by form, and the dead go on doing what the living do — Ovid's underworld is a city with a working day. The full stop Magnus prints after `vitae` is misplaced: `exercent` at the head of the next line is the verb of all three `pars` clauses and the sentence runs straight on. The second witness carries no line at 446 at all.

sentences.t:
Sustinet ire illuc caelesti sede relicta
(tantum odiis iraeque dabat) Saturnia Iuno.
sentences.l: Saturn's daughter Juno brings herself to go there, her heavenly seat having been left behind (so much was she granting to her hatreds and her anger).
sentences.i: Saturn's daughter Juno brought herself to go down there, leaving her seat in heaven — so much she granted to her hatred and her rage.
sentences.n: `caelesti sede relicta` is an ablative absolute: a noun and a participle standing clear of the sentence's own grammar, 'with her heavenly seat left', where English wants a clause. Several more follow in this part. `Sustinet` is 'she brings herself to', a verb of steeling oneself, and the subject arrives only in the last two words — after the parenthesis has explained her.

sentences.t:
Quo simul intravit sacroque a corpore pressum
ingemuit limen, tria Cerberus extulit ora
et tres latratus semel edidit.
sentences.l: As soon as she entered there, and the threshold, pressed by her sacred body, groaned, Cerberus raised his three mouths and gave out three barkings at one stroke.
sentences.i: The moment she stepped in, and the threshold groaned under the weight of a sacred body, Cerberus lifted his three mouths and let out three barks at once.
sentences.n: `Quo` opens the sentence as a connecting relative — 'and there', pointing back to the palace just described. Latin binds sentence to sentence with a relative where English starts fresh with 'and', and you will meet several more here. `simul` stands for `simul ac`, 'as soon as', and governs both verbs. `sacro a corpore pressum` is an ablative of agent with `a`, and it makes the doorstep the thing that registers her arrival: the poem takes the measure of the visit by the weight the stone has to carry.

sentences.t:
Illa sorores
Nocte vocat genitas, grave et inplacabile numen.
Carceris ante fores clausas adamante sedebant
deque suis atros pectebant crinibus angues.
sentences.l: She calls the sisters born of Night, a heavy and unappeasable power. They were sitting before the prison doors, shut with adamant, and combing black snakes out of their own hair.
sentences.i: She calls on the sisters born of Night, a power heavy and not to be appeased. They sat before the prison gates, barred with adamant, combing the black snakes out of their hair.
sentences.n: `Nocte ... genitas` is an ablative of origin with the participle of `gigno`, 'born from Night', wrapped around the noun it belongs to. `numen` is singular for all three of them — one power in three bodies. The imperfects `sedebant` and `pectebant` hold the scene open as something already going on when Juno arrives, and the grooming is domestic on purpose.

sentences.t:
Quam simul agnorunt inter caliginis umbras,
surrexere deae.
sentences.l: As soon as they recognised her among the shadows of the murk, the goddesses rose.
sentences.i: As soon as they made her out among the shadows of that murk, the goddesses rose.
sentences.n: `Quam` is a connecting relative again — 'and her' — carrying Juno across the sentence break. Both perfects are shortened: `agnorunt` for `agnoverunt`, `surrexere` for `surrexerunt`. Ovid calls the Furies `deae` without irony; they are owed the courtesy of standing up.

sentences.t:
Sedes scelerata vocatur:
viscera praebebat Tityos lanianda novemque
iugeribus distentus erat; tibi, Tantale, nullae
deprenduntur aquae, quaeque inminet, effugit arbor;
sentences.l: The place is called Accursed: Tityos was offering his entrails to be torn and was stretched out over nine acres; for you, Tantalus, no waters are caught, and the tree that hangs over you runs away;
sentences.i: The place is called the Accursed Seat. Tityos lay offering his entrails to the tearing, spread over nine acres; for you, Tantalus, no water can be caught, and the tree above you slips away;
sentences.n: `lanianda` is a gerundive, flesh 'to be torn' — the same construction as `laceranda ... viscera` in Juno's speech at 424, though built on a different verb, and here it makes the punishment permanent rather than finished. At `tibi, Tantale` Ovid turns aside and speaks to the sufferer himself: this is apostrophe, direct address to a character in the second person, and it runs on into the next lines. `quaeque` is `quae` plus `-que`, the relative with its conjunction glued on.

sentences.t:
aut petis aut urges rediturum, Sisyphe, saxum;
volvitur Ixion et se sequiturque fugitque;
sentences.l: you either make for or shove the stone that will come back, Sisyphus; Ixion is rolled round, and both follows himself and flees himself;
sentences.i: you are either going after the stone or shoving it up, Sisyphus, and back it will come; Ixion spins, and both chases himself and runs from himself;
sentences.n: The apostrophe carries on to a second sufferer, `Sisyphe`. `rediturum` is a future participle doing the work of an entire clause — the stone 'about to return' — and Ovid sets it before the noun it dooms. Ixion's wheel is never named: `volvitur` is passive, and `se sequitur fugitque` catches the whole circle in four words, one man ahead of himself and behind himself at once.

sentences.t:
molirique suis letum patruelibus ausae
adsiduae repetunt, quas perdant, Belides undas.
sentences.l: and, unremitting, the daughters of Belus, who dared to contrive death for their cousins, fetch back the waters they are to lose.
sentences.i: and the daughters of Belus, who dared to engineer their cousins' death, fetch back without pause the water they are only going to lose.
sentences.n: `ausae` is the perfect participle of the semi-deponent `audeo` — passive in form, active in meaning. `quas perdant` is a relative clause with the subjunctive of purpose or destiny, water fetched *in order to* be lost, and Ovid drops the clause bodily inside the phrase `Belides undas`, so the losing stands between the women and their water. `patruelibus` is precise: cousins on the father's side, the sons of their uncle.

sentences.t:
Quos omnes acie postquam Saturnia torva
vidit et ante omnes Ixiona, rursus ab illo
Sisyphon adspiciens
sentences.l: After Saturn's daughter had seen all these with grim glance, and before all the rest Ixion, looking back from him to Sisyphus,
sentences.i: When Saturn's daughter had looked them all over with a grim eye — Ixion before all the rest — and turned her gaze back from him to Sisyphus,
sentences.n: Another connecting relative, `Quos`, and this one is thrown out in front of its own `postquam`: Latin lets the conjunction sit inside its clause instead of opening it. `acie ... torva` is an ablative of manner split around the subject, `acies` being the edge of a look as well as of a blade. Ixion holds her eye first, `ante omnes`, and the poem does not say why.

sentences.t:
“cur hic e fratribus” inquit
“perpetuas patitur poenas, Athamanta superbum
regia dives habet, qui me cum coniuge semper
sprevit?”
sentences.l: 'Why does this one out of the brothers,' she says, 'suffer punishments without end, [while] a rich palace holds proud Athamas, who together with his wife has always scorned me?'
sentences.i: 'Why does this brother suffer punishment without end,' she says, 'while a rich palace keeps proud Athamas — who, with his wife beside him, has always scorned me?'
sentences.n: The two halves are set side by side with no conjunction between them — asyndeton — and English has to supply 'while' to keep the balance; the loaded word is `dives`, a rich palace weighed against an eternal rock. `e fratribus` assumes the reader knows what Juno knows, that Sisyphus and Athamas are brothers. `me cum coniuge` can go two ways and the line does not settle it: `cum` with the ablative of accompaniment normally attaches to the subject, giving 'who, along with his wife, has always scorned me' — which is what we have just watched Ino do at 420–421, and it puts her among the accused before Juno ever names her — while read the other way it would be 'scorned me along with my husband'. No possessive is written for `coniuge`, which is what leaves it open.

sentences.t:
et exponit causas odiique viaeque,
quidque velit. Quod vellet, erat, ne regia Cadmi
staret, et in facinus traherent Athamanta sorores.
sentences.l: and she sets out the causes both of her hatred and of her journey, and what she wants. What she wanted was this: that the palace of Cadmus should not stand, and that the sisters should draw Athamas into crime.
sentences.i: and she lays out the grounds of her hatred and of her journey, and what she wants. What she wanted was that the house of Cadmus should not stand, and that the sisters should drag Athamas into crime.
sentences.n: `quid velit` keeps a present subjunctive because the narrating verb `exponit` is present; one word later `quod vellet` has slipped to the imperfect because `erat` is past. The tense of an indirect question follows its governing verb, and Ovid lets the reader watch it shift inside a single sentence. `ne ... staret` and `traherent` are the content of the wish, subjunctive because they are what she asks for, not what happened.

sentences.t:
Imperium, promissa, preces confundit in unum
sollicitatque deas.
sentences.l: Command, promises, entreaties she pours together into one, and works upon the goddesses.
sentences.i: Command, promises, entreaties — she runs them all into one, and works on the goddesses.
sentences.n: Three nouns with no conjunctions and then the verb: the asyndeton is the argument, three kinds of pressure applied at once and indistinguishably. `confundo` is literally to pour together. `sollicito` is to shake something loose from its place, and it is the standing word for tampering with someone's loyalty.

sentences.t:
Sic haec Iunone locuta,
Tisiphone, canos ut erat turbata capillos,
movit et obstantes reiecit ab ore colubras
atque ita
sentences.l: Juno having thus spoken these things, Tisiphone — dishevelled as she was as to her grey hair — shook and threw back from her face the snakes that were in the way, and thus [said]:
sentences.i: When Juno had said all this, Tisiphone, dishevelled as she was about her grey hair, shook back from her face the snakes that were in its way, and said:
sentences.n: `Iunone locuta` is an ablative absolute built on a deponent participle, so it is active in sense: 'Juno having spoken'. `turbata ... capillos` is the Greek accusative of respect — a passive participle qualified by an accusative naming the part affected, 'disordered *as to* her hair' — a Greek turn Latin verse borrowed wholesale; it comes back at 546. `movit` and `reiecit` share the one object, `colubras`.

sentences.t:
“non longis opus est ambagibus” inquit:
“facta puta, quaecumque iubes. Inamabile regnum
desere teque refer caeli melioris ad auras.”
sentences.l: 'There is no need of long roundabout ways,' she says: 'reckon done whatever you order. Leave this unlovable kingdom and take yourself back to the air of a better sky.'
sentences.i: 'No need of long circuits,' she says. 'Count it done, whatever you order. Leave this unlovely kingdom and take yourself back to the air of a kinder sky.'
sentences.n: `opus est` takes an ablative of the thing needed, here `ambagibus`, the roundabout ways of speech the Fury is refusing to use. `facta puta` is an imperative with a participle where English wants a clause: 'reckon them done'. Her courtesy is exact and chilling — she does not ask what the order is.

sentences.t:
Laeta redit Iuno, quam caelum intrare parantem
roratis lustravit aquis Thaumantias Iris.
sentences.l: Juno returns glad, and Thaumas's daughter Iris cleansed her with dewy waters as she was preparing to enter heaven.
sentences.i: Juno goes back glad; and as she made ready to enter heaven, Iris, Thaumas's daughter, washed her clean with dewfall.
sentences.n: `quam` is a connecting relative once more — 'and her' — with `parantem` agreeing with it, so that a participle carries what English opens out into a clause. `Thaumantias` is a patronymic, 'daughter of Thaumas', a standing poetic name for Iris. The sprinkling is about pollution: a goddess who has been down there does not re-enter heaven unwashed.

sentences.t:
Nec mora, Tisiphone madefactam sanguine sumit
inportuna facem, fluidoque cruore rubentem
induitur pallam tortoque incingitur angue
egrediturque domo.
sentences.l: And no delay: relentless Tisiphone takes up a torch soaked in blood, and clothes herself in a mantle red with running gore, and girds herself with a twisted snake, and goes out from the house.
sentences.i: No delay: Tisiphone, who spares no one, takes up a torch soaked in blood, puts on a mantle red with running gore, belts a twisted snake about her, and comes out of the house.
sentences.n: `induitur pallam` and `incingitur angue` are the middle use of the passive: the verb is passive in form but the subject is acting on herself, and an accusative of the garment can follow — 'she gets herself into a mantle'. `inportuna` is held over the line-end away from `Tisiphone`, so the epithet lands only after we have seen the torch. `Nec mora` is a two-word verbless sentence, Ovid's usual way of cutting short the delay he is denying.

sentences.t:
Luctus comitatur euntem
et Pavor et Terror trepidoque Insania vultu.
sentences.l: Grief accompanies her as she goes, and Dread and Terror and Madness with trembling face.
sentences.i: Grief goes with her as she goes, and Dread and Terror, and Madness with its shivering face.
sentences.n: Four abstractions given bodies and a walking pace; Latin can turn a common noun into a person without altering a letter, which is why editors have to decide where to put the capital. `euntem` is the participle of `eo` used bare, as a noun with no noun to lean on — 'the one going'. `trepido vultu` is an ablative of description hung on `Insania` and placed last, so the reader is left with the face.

sentences.t:
Limine constiterat: postes tremuisse feruntur
Aeolii pallorque fores infecit acernas,
solque locum fugit.
sentences.l: She had halted on the threshold: the Aeolian doorposts are said to have trembled, and pallor stained the maple doors, and the sun fled the place.
sentences.i: She had halted on the threshold. The doorposts of Aeolus's house are said to have shuddered; a pallor came over the maple doors, and the sun fled the place.
sentences.n: `feruntur ... tremuisse` is the personal construction of 'they say': the doorposts themselves are the subject of the passive and take an infinitive, where English says 'they say the posts trembled'. `Aeolii` is held over to the next line, so the house is identified only after it has shaken. Every omen here is a withdrawal of light.

sentences.t:
Monstris exterrita coniunx,
territus est Athamas.
sentences.l: The wife [was] terrified by the portents, Athamas was terrified.
sentences.i: The wife was terrified by these portents; Athamas was terrified.
sentences.n: One verb twice in two forms, `exterrita` and `territus est`, with the two people set on either side of it — the balance is the whole sentence. The first half has no verb at all: the `est` of the second does duty for both, which Latin permits and English will not.

sentences.t:
Tectoque exire parabant:
obstitit infelix aditumque obsedit Erinys,
nexaque vipereis distendens bracchia nodis
caesariem excussit.
sentences.l: And they were preparing to go out of the house: the baleful Fury stood in the way and blockaded the exit, and, spreading wide her arms bound with viper-knots, shook out her hair.
sentences.i: They were making to leave the house: the baleful Fury stood in the way and shut off the door, and, spreading wide her arms in their knotted vipers, shook out her hair.
sentences.n: `infelix` here is the older, harder sense — bringing no increase, unlucky to meet — not 'unhappy'. `bracchia` is the plain object of `distendens`, with `nexa ... nodis` a participle agreeing with it — arms 'knotted with vipers', `nodus` being the ordinary word for the knot in a rope, so the snakes are described as cordage. `aditus` is the way in, and from inside the house it is the way out; `obsedit` is a siege word, and the door is now under siege.

sentences.t:
Motae sonuere colubrae,
parsque iacent umeris, pars circum pectora lapsae
sibila dant saniemque vomunt linguisque coruscant.
sentences.l: The snakes, set moving, sounded; and part lie on her shoulders, part, having slid about her breast, give hissings and vomit corruption and flicker with their tongues.
sentences.i: The snakes, once stirred, made their noise: some lie along her shoulders, some, sliding about her breast, hiss, vomit their foulness, and flicker their tongues.
sentences.n: `sonuere` is `sonuerunt`, the short perfect again. `pars ... iacent` takes its plural verb by sense, exactly as at 444. The three verbs run out one after another at the end with no build-up, `dant`, `vomunt`, `coruscant`: Ovid lets the hair go on doing things after the sentence would naturally have stopped.

sentences.t:
Inde duos mediis abrumpit crinibus angues
pestiferaque manu raptos inmisit. At illi
Inoosque sinus Athamanteosque pererrant
inspirantque graves animas.
sentences.l: Then she tears two snakes away from the middle of her hair and, once snatched, sent them in with her plague-bearing hand. But they wander over the breast of Ino and of Athamas and breathe heavy breaths into them.
sentences.i: Then she tears two snakes out of the middle of her hair and, catching them up, flung them with her plague-bearing hand. They range across Ino's breast and Athamas's and breathe their heavy breath into them.
sentences.n: `abrumpit` is present and `inmisit` perfect inside one sentence: the historic present brings the tearing up close, the perfect drops the throw behind us, and Ovid alternates the two through this whole scene to change its speed. `Inoos` and `Athamanteos` are adjectives coined off the two names, so the snakes cross not 'the breast of Ino' but an Ino-ish breast; the `-que ... -que` pairing binds husband and wife into a single target.

sentences.t:
Nec vulnera membris
ulla ferunt: mens est, quae diros sentiat ictus.
sentences.l: Nor do they bring any wounds to the limbs: it is the mind that feels the dreadful blows.
sentences.i: They bring no wound to the body at all: it is the mind that feels the dreadful blows.
sentences.n: `quae ... sentiat` is a relative clause with the subjunctive of characteristic — 'the sort of thing that feels' — and after `mens est` it works as a definition: the mind is precisely the part that takes the damage. The line is the hinge of the episode. Nothing whatever is done to these two bodies, and everything that follows comes out of that.

sentences.t:
Attulerat secum liquidi quoque monstra veneni,
oris Cerberei spumas et virus Echidnae
erroresque vagos caecaeque oblivia mentis
et scelus et lacrimas rabiemque et caedis amorem,
sentences.l: She had also brought with her the monstrous stuff of liquid poison: foam of Cerberus's mouth and the venom of Echidna, and wandering delusions and the forgettings of a blinded mind, and crime and tears and rage and love of slaughter,
sentences.i: She had brought liquid poison too, monstrous stuff: foam from Cerberus's mouth, Echidna's venom, wandering delusion, the blank forgetfulness of a darkened mind — and crime, and tears, and rage, and the love of killing,
sentences.n: `quoque` here is the plain adverb 'also'; it is worth testing each time, since the same letters can be `quō-que`, 'and with which'. The list begins with things that can be poured — foam, venom — and slides without warning into things that cannot: delusion, crime, tears, the love of killing, all made pourable by the grammar that holds them. `caecae mentis` is blind in the sense of unable to see: the mind's own darkness, not another's.

sentences.t:
omnia trita simul; quae sanguine mixta recenti
coxerat aere cavo viridi versata cicuta.
sentences.l: all ground up together; and these, mixed with fresh blood, she had boiled in hollow bronze, stirred with green hemlock.
sentences.i: all ground together; and these she had mixed with fresh blood and boiled in hollow bronze, stirring them with green hemlock.
sentences.n: `quae` opens the clause as a connecting relative, 'and these'. `mixta` and `versata` are perfect participles agreeing with it, packed round the single finite verb `coxerat`, so the whole recipe hangs off one 'she had boiled'. The hemlock is the spoon: a poison used to stir the poison.

sentences.t:
Dumque pavent illi, vergit furiale venenum
pectus in amborum praecordiaque intima movit.
sentences.l: And while they cower, she tips the maddening poison into the breast of them both, and stirred their innermost vitals.
sentences.i: And while the two of them stood cowering, she tipped the maddening venom into both their breasts and set their inmost parts moving.
sentences.n: `dum` with a present indicative means 'while' even when the story around it is in the past. `pectus in amborum` puts the preposition inside its own phrase, between the noun and the genitive depending on it — ordinary in verse, impossible in English. `praecordia` are the parts under the heart, where Latin puts feeling rather than thought.

sentences.t:
Tum face iactata per eundem saepius orbem
consequitur motis velociter ignibus ignes.
sentences.l: Then, the torch having been swung again and again through the same circle, she overtakes fires with fires, the flames being moved swiftly.
sentences.i: Then she swings the torch again and again through the same circle, and the flames, moving fast, run one into the next.
sentences.n: `face iactata` is an ablative absolute; `motis ... ignibus` is a plain instrumental ablative, the flames being the means by which fire catches fire. `consequitur ignes` describes what a whirled brand actually looks like: the eye cannot separate one fire from the fire before it, so the ring closes. `saepius` is a comparative used loosely for 'again and again', a common poetic softening.

sentences.t:
Sic victrix iussique potens ad inania magni
regna redit Ditis sumptumque recingitur anguem.
sentences.l: So, victorious and in command of her order, she returns to the empty realms of great Dis and ungirds the snake she had taken up.
sentences.i: So, victorious and mistress of her commission, she goes back to the empty realms of great Dis and unbelts the snake she had put on.
sentences.n: `potens` takes a genitive of the thing one has power over — `iussi`, the order she was given — so 'having her orders in hand'. `recingitur anguem` is the middle voice again, answering `incingitur angue` at 483: she takes off precisely what she put on, and the episode closes like a buckle. `inania regna` is the standing epithet of the world of shades, empty because its people have no bodies.

sentences.t:
Protinus Aeolides media furibundus in aula
clamat “io, comites, his retia tendite silvis!
hic modo cum gemina visa est mihi prole leaena:”
sentences.l: At once the son of Aeolus, raving in the middle of the hall, shouts: 'Ho, companions, stretch the nets in these woods! Here just now a lioness with twin young was seen by me:'
sentences.i: At once the son of Aeolus, raving in the middle of his own hall, shouts: 'Ho there, companions — spread the nets in this wood! A lioness with two cubs was in sight here a moment ago!'
sentences.n: `Aeolides` is a patronymic, 'son of Aeolus': the poem names Athamas by his father at the moment he stops being a father himself. The madness is specific rather than general — he is not seeing nothing, he is seeing a hunt, and his hall has become woodland. `gemina prole` is 'twofold offspring', which is what he has: two sons.

sentences.t:
utque ferae sequitur vestigia coniugis amens
deque sinu matris ridentem et parva Learchum
bracchia tendentem rapit et bis terque per auras
more rotat fundae rigidoque infantia saxo
discutit ora ferox.
sentences.l: and out of his mind he follows the tracks of his wife as of a wild beast, and from the mother's lap he snatches Learchus, laughing and stretching out his little arms, and twice and three times whirls him through the air in the manner of a sling, and savagely dashes the infant face to pieces on the hard rock.
sentences.i: and out of his mind he follows his wife's tracks as a wild beast's; and from his mother's lap he snatches Learchus, who is laughing and holding out his small arms, and whirls him twice and three times through the air like a stone in a sling, and savagely shatters the baby's face on the hard rock.
sentences.n: `ferae ... coniugis` is one phrase, 'of his wife the beast': the madness is in the grammar, an apposition that turns her into an animal without saying so. `ridentem` and `bracchia tendentem` both agree with `Learchum` and are both held back until after `rapit`, so the child is shown to us only as he is being taken. `more fundae` is the sling — a stone whirled on a thong before release — and `infantia ora` sets the word for a child who cannot yet speak beside the word for a mouth.

sentences.t:
Tum denique concita mater,
seu dolor hoc fecit seu sparsi causa veneni,
exululat passisque fugit male sana capillis
sentences.l: Then at last the mother, driven wild — whether grief did this, or the sprinkled poison was the cause — shrieks aloud and flees, hardly sane, with her hair let loose,
sentences.i: Then at last the mother, driven wild — whether grief did it, or the poison sprinkled on her was the cause — shrieks out and runs, scarcely in her senses, her hair let down,
sentences.n: `seu ... seu` leaves the cause genuinely open and the poem never comes back to settle it: the reader is asked to hold both. `passis capillis` is an ablative absolute on the participle of `pando`, 'spread out'; loosened hair is the sign of mourning and of ritual frenzy at once, which is exactly why it can stand here. `male sana` is 'badly sound', the Latin way of saying not right in the head.

sentences.t:
teque ferens parvum nudis, Melicerta, lacertis
“euhoe Bacche” sonat.
sentences.l: and carrying you, little Melicerta, on her bare arms, she sounds out 'euhoe, Bacchus!'
sentences.i: and carrying you, little Melicerta, on her bare arms, she cries out 'euhoe, Bacchus!'
sentences.n: Ovid turns and speaks to the child directly — apostrophe again, as with Tantalus and Sisyphus at 458–460, but those two were addressed across a distance and this child is being carried past us. `euhoe` is the ritual shout of Bacchus's worshippers rather than a word with a meaning, and Ino's madness comes out of her as the god's own cry. `sonat` takes the shout as its object: she sounds it.

sentences.t:
Bacchi sub nomine Iuno
risit et “hos usus praestet tibi” dixit “alumnus.”
sentences.l: At the name of Bacchus Juno laughed and said: 'may your nursling furnish you services like these.'
sentences.i: At the name of Bacchus Juno laughed, and said: 'may that nursling of yours do you services like these.'
sentences.n: `alumnus` is the last word of the sentence and the point of it: it picks up `alumno numine` from line 421, the nursling god who was the last and worst item on the list of Ino's grounds for pride, and hands it back to her. `hos usus` is 'these good offices', said with the knife in; `praestet` is a jussive subjunctive, a wish shaped exactly like a blessing and functioning as a curse. `sub nomine` is 'at the sound of the name' — the name is what sets her laughing.

sentences.t:
Inminet aequoribus scopulus: pars ima cavatur
fluctibus et tectas defendit ab imbribus undas,
summa riget frontemque in apertum porrigit aequor.
sentences.l: A crag overhangs the waters: its lowest part is hollowed out by the waves and shields the covered water from the rains; the top stands stiff and stretches its forehead out into the open sea.
sentences.i: A crag overhangs the water: the foot of it is hollowed by the waves and shields the water it covers from the rain; the top stands rigid and thrusts its brow out over the open sea.
sentences.n: `pars ima` and `summa` are the adjectives 'lowest' and 'highest' used to mean 'the lowest part of', a Latin habit English has to unpack every time. `defendit` has `undas` for its object and `ab imbribus` for what is warded away — the ordinary 'protect X from Y' — and `tectas` is proleptic: the hollowing is what makes the water covered in the first place, so the adjective describes a state the verb has only just produced. `frontem` gives the rock a face and `porrigit` pushes it out over the sea a full line before Ino arrives: the scenery is built for the leap.

sentences.t:
Occupat hunc (vires insania fecerat) Ino,
seque super pontum nullo tardata timore
mittit onusque suum; percussa recanduit unda.
sentences.l: Ino takes possession of it (madness had made the strength), and, delayed by no fear, launches herself out over the sea, and her own burden; the struck water shone white.
sentences.i: Ino takes it (madness had given her the strength), and, checked by no fear, throws herself out over the sea, and her burden with her; where it struck, the water went white.
sentences.n: `vires insania fecerat` is a whole explanation in three words dropped into a parenthesis — Ovid regularly puts the physics of a marvel in brackets. `onus suum`, 'her own burden', is the child, and the poem will not use his name at the moment she jumps. `recanduit` carries the inceptive force of `-sco`: the water 'went white', the foam opening where the two of them hit it.

sentences.t:
At Venus, inmeritae neptis miserata labores,
sic patruo blandita suo est: “O numen aquarum,
proxima cui caelo cessit, Neptune, potestas,
magna quidem posco, sed tu miserere meorum,
sentences.l: But Venus, having pitied the sufferings of her undeserving granddaughter, coaxed her uncle thus: 'O divine power of the waters, Neptune, to whom the power next after heaven fell, great things indeed I ask, but do you pity my own,
sentences.i: But Venus, moved by the sufferings of a granddaughter who had not earned them, coaxed her uncle so: 'O godhead of the waters, Neptune, to whom fell the power that comes next after heaven's — great things I ask, I grant it, but pity my own,
sentences.n: `miserata` and `blandita` are deponent participles, passive in form and active in sense, and `blandior` takes the dative (`patruo suo`), because in Latin coaxing is done *to* someone. `inmeritae` means undeserving of what she is suffering, not undeserving of help. Venus's whole case is kinship on both sides at once: `neptis` makes Ino her granddaughter, `patruus` is precisely a father's brother.

sentences.t:
iactari quos cernis in Ionio inmenso,
et dis adde tuis. Aliqua et mihi gratia ponto est,
si tamen in medio quondam concreta profundo
spuma fui Graiumque manet mihi nomen ab illa.”
sentences.l: whom you see being tossed on the measureless Ionian, and add them to your own gods. I too have some favour with the sea, if indeed I was once foam, curdled in the middle of the deep, and my Greek name remains to me from that.'
sentences.i: whom you see tossed on the measureless Ionian — and add them to your gods. I too have some claim upon the sea, if it is true that I was once foam, curdled in mid-ocean, and that my Greek name still comes to me from it.'
sentences.n: `iactari quos cernis` is accusative and infinitive after a verb of perceiving, 'you see them being tossed', with the infinitive thrown out in front of the relative that is its own subject. The last sentence is the argument, and it turns on a name: Venus's Greek name is built on the Greek for foam, so she is asking the sea to honour its own etymology. `si tamen` is 'if, that is' — a polite hedge over a claim she has no intention of withdrawing.

sentences.t:
Adnuit oranti Neptunus et abstulit illis,
quod mortale fuit, maiestatemque verendam
inposuit
sentences.l: Neptune nodded assent to her as she prayed, and took away from them what was mortal, and laid on them a majesty to be revered,
sentences.i: Neptune nodded to her prayer, and took from them what was mortal in them, and laid on them a majesty to be feared,
sentences.n: `adnuo` is to nod towards, the physical gesture of assent, and it takes a dative: `oranti`, 'to her praying', a participle standing in for a whole clause. `quod mortale fuit` is the object of `abstulit`, a neuter relative used as a noun — 'the mortal part'. `verendam` is a gerundive, 'to be revered', and Latin does not separate that from 'to be feared': one word covers both.

sentences.t:
nomenque simul faciemque novavit
Leucothoeque deum cum matre Palaemona dixit.
sentences.l: and made new at one stroke both their name and their face, and called the god Palaemon along with his mother Leucothoe.
sentences.i: and made new at one stroke both name and form, and called the god Palaemon, and his mother with him Leucothoe.
sentences.n: `novavit` governs both nouns and `simul` insists on the simultaneity: in this poem a change of shape and a change of name are one event. Both new names carry their sense in Greek — Leucothoe is the white goddess, and the white is the water that closed over her at 530; Palaemon is a wrestler's name. `deum` is the accusative of `deus` in apposition to `Palaemona`, which keeps its Greek ending.

sentences.t:
Sidoniae comites, quantum valuere secutae
signa pedum, primo videre novissima saxo;
sentences.l: Her Sidonian companions, having followed the marks of her feet as far as they had strength for, saw the last of them at the rock's edge;
sentences.i: Her Sidonian companions followed the prints of her feet as far as they could, and saw the last of them at the lip of the rock;
sentences.n: `valuere` and `videre` are both the short third-plural perfect, two of them within two lines. `Sidoniae` marks the women as Cadmus's people, Phoenicians settled at Thebes. `novissima` is the superlative of `novus` in its everyday Latin sense of 'last', not 'newest' — the prints that stop at the edge — and `primo saxo` works the same way as `pars ima` at 525, the adjective naming the part: 'at the near edge of the rock'.

sentences.t:
nec dubium de morte ratae Cadmeida palmis
deplanxere domum, scissae cum veste capillos,
sentences.l: and having reckoned there was no doubt about her death, they beat their hands and wailed for the house of Cadmus, torn as to their hair along with their clothing,
sentences.i: and, reckoning her death beyond doubt, they beat their hands and keened for the house of Cadmus, their hair torn and their garments with it,
sentences.n: `scissae ... capillos` is the Greek accusative of respect once more, as at 474: 'torn as to their hair'. `cum veste` then hangs a second thing on the same participle, so a single word covers hair and dress together. `Cadmeida` is a Greek accusative form, `deplanxere` another short perfect, and `ratae` the deponent participle of `reor`, active in sense.

sentences.t:
utque parum iustae nimiumque in paelice saevae
invidiam fecere deae.
sentences.l: and they made ill-will against the goddess as too little just and too savage in the matter of a mistress.
sentences.i: and they raised feeling against the goddess, as too little just and far too savage in the matter of a mistress.
sentences.n: `paelex` is the hard word again — the other woman — and it is doing something odd here, because it belongs to Juno's vocabulary and not to these women's, and the object of the savagery is Ino, who was never Jupiter's. The mourners appear to be quoting the grudge back at the goddess who holds it. `invidiam facere` with a dative is a phrase out of public life, to make somebody unpopular; `fecere` is `fecerunt`.

sentences.t:
Convicia Iuno
non tulit et “faciam vos ipsas maxima” dixit
“saevitiae monimenta meae.” Res dicta secuta est.
sentences.l: Juno did not bear the abuse, and said: 'I will make you yourselves the greatest memorials of my savagery.' The outcome followed the words spoken.
sentences.i: Juno did not bear the abuse. 'I will make you yourselves,' she said, 'the greatest memorials of my savagery.' The outcome followed the words.
sentences.n: Juno picks up the charge — `saevitia`, savagery — and adopts it as her own word, which is the cruellest thing in the sentence. `monimenta` is whatever makes a thing remembered, so the women are to become the standing proof of the accusation they made. In `Res dicta secuta est`, `secuta est` is the deponent `sequor` and takes `dicta`, neuter plural, as its object: the thing that happened follows the things that were said, and four words with no connective shut the speech like a lid.

sentences.t:
Nam quae praecipue fuerat pia, “persequar” inquit
“in freta reginam” saltumque datura moveri
haud usquam potuit scopuloque adfixa cohaesit.
sentences.l: For she who had been loyal above the rest says, 'I will follow the queen into the sea,' and, about to give a leap, could not be moved anywhere at all, and clung fast, fixed to the rock.
sentences.i: For the one who had been loyal above the rest says, 'I will follow the queen into the water' — and, on the point of leaping, could not be moved at all, but clung there, fixed to the rock.
sentences.n: `datura` is a future participle used of something on the very point of happening, 'about to make her jump': the leap is suspended in the grammar exactly as it is in the body. `moveri` is passive — she cannot even be moved, let alone move — and `haud usquam` denies her any direction whatever. `pia` is loyalty owed and paid, the same word used of duty to gods and to family.

sentences.t:
Altera, dum solito temptat plangore ferire
pectora, temptatos sensit riguisse lacertos;
sentences.l: Another, while she tries to strike her breast with the accustomed beating, felt that the arms she had tried had stiffened;
sentences.i: Another, while she tried to beat her breast with the accustomed blow, felt that the arms she was trying had gone stiff;
sentences.n: `temptat` and `temptatos` are one verb used twice, once of her attempt and once of the arms attempted; the repetition is both the wit and the horror. `sensit riguisse` is accusative and infinitive after a verb of perceiving, and the perfect infinitive shows the stiffening already complete before she notices it. `plangor` is the formal beating of the breast in mourning, which is why it can be `solito`, the accustomed one.

sentences.t:
illa, manus ut forte tetenderat in maris undas,
saxea facta manus in easdem porrigit undas;
sentences.l: that one, as she happened to have stretched her hands out toward the sea's waves, made of stone, holds her hands out to those same waves;
sentences.i: another, having chanced to stretch her hands towards the waves of the sea, is turned to stone, and holds those hands out still to the same waves;
sentences.n: The sentence repeats itself on purpose — `manus ... in maris undas`, then `manus in easdem ... undas` — so that its second half is its first half frozen. `forte`, 'as it happened', carries the cruelty of the whole passage: the posture each woman is fixed in was an accident. `saxea facta` agrees with the woman herself, not with the hands.

sentences.t:
huius, ut arreptum laniabat vertice crinem,
duratos subito digitos in crine videres:
quo quaeque in gestu deprensa est, haesit in illo.
sentences.l: of this one, as she was tearing at the hair she had seized from the crown of her head, you would see the fingers suddenly hardened in the hair: in whatever gesture each was caught, in that she stuck fast.
sentences.i: of another, as she tore at the hair she had seized from her head, you would have seen her fingers suddenly hardened in it: in whatever gesture each one was caught, in that gesture she stuck.
sentences.n: `videres` is a potential subjunctive with an indefinite 'you' — 'one would have seen' — which puts the reader at the scene without claiming they were there. `huius` is a genitive left hanging at the head of the sentence and picked up only much later by `digitos`, a loose join that verse allows. The last line states the rule the whole catalogue has been illustrating, and its halves answer each other word for word: `quo ... in gestu` against `in illo`.

sentences.t:
Pars volucres factae; quae nunc quoque gurgite in illo
aequora destringunt summis Ismenides alis.
sentences.l: Part were made birds; and these, the Ismenides, even now in that gulf skim the waters with the tips of their wings.
sentences.i: Some were made birds; and these, the women of Ismenus, even now skim that gulf, brushing the water with their wingtips.
sentences.n: `pars ... factae` again takes its agreement by sense, and `quae` is a connecting relative, 'and these'. `quoque` is once more the adverb, not `quō-que`: `nunc quoque`, 'even now', is Ovid's regular formula for bringing a metamorphosis up to the reader's own day, so that the tale ends in something still there to be seen. The name `Ismenides` — women of the Theban river Ismenus — is saved for the very last word, after the birds are already in the air.

questions: Quotable line, IV.428: `fas est et ab hoste doceri`. No house rendering exists for it, so one was built from the Latin and shipped. Shipped l: 'it is right to be taught even by an enemy'; shipped i: 'it is right to be taught even by an enemy' (identical inside the unit's wider sentence). Please ratify or replace.

Quotable line, IV.550: `Res dicta secuta est`. Shipped l: 'The outcome followed the words spoken.'; shipped i: 'The outcome followed the words.' (Review flattened the drafter's 'The deed followed hard on the word' — 'followed hard on' has the cadence of an anthology quotation rather than of anything derived from these four words, and the plainer version is what the Latin gives.) Recorded for ratification rather than re-decided later.

Possible quotable line, IV.499: `mens est, quae diros sentiat ictus`. Shipped l: 'it is the mind that feels the dreadful blows'; shipped i is the same clause. Flagged in case it wants fixing as a house rendering, since it is the sententia the whole episode turns on.

PRECEDENT-SETTING, needs a human ruling. Advisory at IV.515-519 (killing of Learchus, graphic-detail trigger, string form): the drafter shipped one; review REMOVED it, and the part now carries no advisory at all. The drafter's case for shipping, in full: 'the contract says the trigger fires rarely and a close call is a no, and this was close. It was shipped because the poem does not merely report a killing — it names the instrument by simile (more ... fundae), names the body part destroyed (infantia ... ora), and picks the verb of shattering (discutit), after four lines that put the child in our hands laughing and reaching. That is specific bodily damage held in focus rather than ordinary killing passed over.' Review's case for removing: the contract's trigger is that the text STOPS TO DWELL on bodily damage in specific detail, and this text does not stop. The damage occupies half a line — `rigidoque infantia saxo / discutit ora ferox` — and the sentence moves straight on to Ino at `Tum denique`. What Ovid does dwell on is the child's laughing and his outstretched arms, which is pathos, and the sling, which is the manner of the throw; neither is bodily damage. Nothing is described of the body after the rock. The contract also says in terms that ordinary killing and dismemberment earn nothing, and that a close call is a no — and the drafter's own reasoning opens by conceding this was close, which under the rule as written settles it against shipping. Countervailing consideration a human should weigh: the contract's own live example of the string form (Lycaon's boiled limbs) is likewise only two lines long, so brevity alone may not be the discriminator the removal leans on; if the ruling is that a victim who is an infant plus a named instrument of destruction is enough, the drafter's advisory should be restored verbatim. No other trigger fires in this part.
Variant IV.437 noted in the note on 436-438: Magnus `qua ducat`, second witness `quod ducat` — it changes the construction of the indirect question and so the sense.

Variant IV.446 noted in the note on 443-446: the second witness carries no line there. The line supplies `exercent`, the verb of all three `pars` clauses, so a reader would feel its absence; the more likely explanation is a line-numbering offset in the second witness rather than a real omission, and that is worth checking against the mirror.

Variants IV.443 (`et`/`at`), IV.460 (`urges`/`urgues`) and IV.488 (`exterrita`/`est territa`) were judged not sense-changing and left unnoted — orthography and morphology. 443 in particular looks like an alignment artefact, since `at` will not construe in Magnus's line.

Punctuation fault in the digitization, not a damaged word: Magnus's text as supplied prints a full stop after `vitae` at the end of 445 and no stop at the end of 446, which breaks the sentence at the wrong place. The text is printed unaltered and the note on 443-446 says so; no emendation made.

Homograph for the shared glossary, IV.437: `manes` here is the noun, the shades of the dead (nominative plural), not the second-person present of `maneo`, which occurs in this same part at 538 (`manet`).
Homograph for the shared glossary, IV.450 and IV.519: `ora` here is the plural of `os, oris`, mouths (450) and face (519), not `ora, -ae`, shore or coastline, and not the imperative of `oro`.
Homograph for the shared glossary, IV.497: `sinus` here is the breast or bosom of a person, not a bay or an inlet of the sea, which is the sense the same form usually carries elsewhere in this poem.
No intra-word digitization damage of the `adfiatu`/`cuuis` kind was found anywhere in IV.416-562; every form parses as Latin.

Review verified both of the drafter's claims about 445/446 independently against the supplied text file, and both hold: the file does print `... antiquae imitamina vitae.` with a full stop at the end of 445 and `exercent, aliam partem sua poena coercet` with no terminal stop at the end of 446, so the sentence is broken one word before its own verb; and the variants file does show the second witness carrying nothing at all at 446. No repair was made to `t`. The drafter's guess in its own note — that this is more likely a line-numbering offset in the mirror than a genuine omission — is plausible and unverified, and the reader-facing note states the absence as fact; a human may want that clause softened to the contract's standard form.

READING CHANGED BY REVIEW, IV.468: `qui me cum coniuge semper sprevit`. The drafter shipped 'who has always scorned me together with my husband' and its note ruled the alternative out. Review reversed it to 'who together with his wife has always scorned me', because `cum` + ablative of accompaniment normally attaches to the subject, `coniuge` carries no possessive to pull it towards Juno, and the lines immediately before (420–421: Ino proud of her children, of the marriage-chamber of Athamas, and of the god she nursed) show the couple slighting Juno together, which is also what her stated wish at 470–471 goes on to attack. The note now gives both readings and says the line does not settle it. Worth a ruling, since it decides whether Ino stands accused in Juno's own speech.

Segmentation, IV.541: the unit boundary between `... maiestatemque verendam / inposuit` and `nomenque simul faciemque novavit` falls mid-line at no punctuation — the only such split in the part. Left as the drafter set it rather than merged, because merging would fold two units and two notes into one; flagged so the lineation convention can be applied deliberately.

Gloss decision, IV.423: `vertere` is taken as the bare verb of metamorphosis (no complement, new shape unstated), so the idiomatic reads 'transform' where the drafter had 'turn', which in English reads as turning the sailors around. The literal keeps 'turn'.
